results.name: rule_member_out_minus_in_range
results.description: For sets of >=3 examples consistent with a parity or multiples-of-m (3-12) rule, among non-example targets that belong to the smallest such consistent rule, yes rate outside the examples' min-max range minus inside; the model's rule/interval mixture predicts a negative gap, so observed above null means people extend broad arithmetic rules beyond the example range as readily as within it (e.g. 63,27,99,33 -> 3; 69,9,39,21 -> 72-96).
results.code:
# name: rule_member_out_minus_in_range
# description: For sets of >=3 examples consistent with a parity or multiples-of-m (3-12) rule, among non-example targets that belong to the smallest such consistent rule, yes rate outside the examples' min-max range minus inside; the model's rule/interval mixture predicts a negative gap, so observed above null means people extend broad arithmetic rules beyond the example range as readily as within it (e.g. 63,27,99,33 -> 3; 69,9,39,21 -> 72-96).
def test_statistic(df):
    N = np.arange(1, 101)
    rules = [N % 2 == 0, N % 2 == 1] + [N % m == 0 for m in range(3, 13)]
    M = np.array(rules); sizes = M.sum(axis=1)
    s_arr = df["number_set"].astype(str).to_numpy()
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    ins = np.zeros(len(df), bool); out = np.zeros(len(df), bool)
    for s in np.unique(s_arr):
        e = np.array([int(x) for x in s.split(",")])
        if len(e) < 3:
            continue
        ok = M[:, e - 1].all(axis=1)
        if not ok.any():
            continue
        i = np.where(ok)[0][np.argmin(sizes[ok])]
        idx = (s_arr == s) & M[i][t - 1] & ~np.isin(t, e)
        inr = (t >= e.min()) & (t <= e.max())
        ins |= idx & inr; out |= idx & ~inr
    if ins.sum() == 0 or out.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[out].mean() - r[ins].mean())

results.name: shared_digit_nonmember_inside_minus_outside
results.description: Among unsorted (not monotone) sets of >=3 examples that all share a last digit, yes rate for targets lacking that digit that lie inside the examples' min-max range minus those outside it; the model's interval component predicts a positive gap, so observed below null means people reject in-range non-members as firmly as out-of-range ones (range adds nothing once a digit rule is clear).

results.name: in_range_opposite_parity_contrast
results.description: For sets of >=3 examples all of one parity that do not all share a last digit, yes rate for in-range (between min and max example) non-example targets of the opposite parity minus same parity; the model's parity-blind intervals predict a small gap, so observed below null means people restrict range generalization to the examples' parity (e.g. 23,35,95,83 rejects even 30-36).
results.code:
# name: in_range_opposite_parity_contrast
# description: For sets of >=3 examples all of one parity that do not all share a last digit, yes rate for in-range (between min and max example) non-example targets of the opposite parity minus same parity; the model's parity-blind intervals predict a small gap, so observed below null means people restrict range generalization to the examples' parity (e.g. 23,35,95,83 rejects even 30-36).
def test_statistic(df):
    s_arr = df["number_set"].astype(str).to_numpy()
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    opp = np.zeros(len(df), bool); same = np.zeros(len(df), bool)
    for s in np.unique(s_arr):
        e = np.array([int(x) for x in s.split(",")])
        if len(e) < 3 or len(set(e % 2)) != 1 or len(set(e % 10)) == 1:
            continue
        idx = (s_arr == s) & (t >= e.min()) & (t <= e.max()) & ~np.isin(t, e)
        sp = (t % 2) == (e[0] % 2)
        same |= idx & sp; opp |= idx & ~sp
    if opp.sum() == 0 or same.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[opp].mean() - r[same].mean())

results.name: sorted_minus_unsorted_out_of_range
results.description: Among sets of >=3 examples, yes rate for non-example targets outside the examples' min-max range in sorted (strictly monotone) sets minus in unsorted sets; the model's sorted-order shift toward range concepts predicts sorted < unsorted, so observed above null means sorted lists do not make people more range-bound (the order shift is an over-general side effect).
results.code:
# name: sorted_minus_unsorted_out_of_range
# description: Among sets of >=3 examples, yes rate for non-example targets outside the examples' min-max range in sorted (strictly monotone) sets minus in unsorted sets; the model's sorted-order shift toward range concepts predicts sorted < unsorted, so observed above null means sorted lists do not make people more range-bound (the order shift is an over-general side effect).
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce")
    n = ex.notna().sum(axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(int)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float)
    d = ex.diff(axis=1).iloc[:, 1:]
    valid = d.notna()
    inc = ((d > 0) | ~valid).all(axis=1); dec = ((d < 0) | ~valid).all(axis=1)
    srt = (inc | dec) & (n >= 3)
    out = (t < ex.min(axis=1)) | (t > ex.max(axis=1))
    base = (n >= 3) & out
    a = base & srt; b = base & ~srt
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: parity_rule_four_minus_three_examples
results.description: For sets whose examples all share parity but not a last digit, yes rate for same-parity non-example targets in 4-example sets minus 3-example sets; the size principle predicts a positive gap (more examples, stronger parity rule), so observed below null means extra examples do not strengthen (or even weaken) parity generalization as the model predicts.
results.code:
# name: parity_rule_four_minus_three_examples
# description: For sets whose examples all share parity but not a last digit, yes rate for same-parity non-example targets in 4-example sets minus 3-example sets; the size principle predicts a positive gap (more examples, stronger parity rule), so observed below null means extra examples do not strengthen (or even weaken) parity generalization as the model predicts.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce")
    n = ex.notna().sum(axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(int)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float)
    par = ex % 2; last = ex % 10
    uni_par = (par.max(axis=1) == par.min(axis=1))
    uni_last = (last.max(axis=1) == last.min(axis=1))
    inset = ex.eq(t, axis=0).any(axis=1)
    same = (t % 2) == par.iloc[:, 0]
    base = uni_par & ~uni_last & ~inset & same
    a = base & (n == 4); b = base & (n == 3)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: shared_digit_nonmember_late_minus_early
results.description: For sets of >=2 examples all sharing a last digit, yes rate for targets lacking that digit in the second half of the session (trial_index above median) minus the first half; the model is stationary (null ~0), so observed below null means people become stricter about digit rules over the session, above null more lenient.
results.code:
# name: shared_digit_nonmember_late_minus_early
# description: For sets of >=2 examples all sharing a last digit, yes rate for targets lacking that digit in the second half of the session (trial_index above median) minus the first half; the model is stationary (null ~0), so observed below null means people become stricter about digit rules over the session, above null more lenient.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce")
    n = ex.notna().sum(axis=1)
    last = ex % 10
    uni = (last.max(axis=1) == last.min(axis=1)) & (n >= 2)
    t = df["target"].astype(int)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float)
    non = uni & ((t % 10) != last.iloc[:, 0])
    ti = df["trial_index"].astype(float)
    late = ti > ti.median()
    a = non & late; b = non & ~late
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: digit_only_minus_arithmetic_only
results.description: For sets consistent with both a digit rule (ends-in-d / contains-d, all examples) and an arithmetic rule (multiples of 3-12, squares, cubes, primes, powers of 2-10), yes rate for non-example targets satisfying only a consistent digit rule minus targets satisfying only a consistent arithmetic rule (e.g. 8,80,48: 28/68 vs 96; 28,98: x8 vs multiples of 7); observed above null means people favour digit rules over equally-consistent arithmetic rules more than the model's size-principle weighting allows.
results.code:
# name: digit_only_minus_arithmetic_only
# description: For sets consistent with both a digit rule (ends-in-d / contains-d, all examples) and an arithmetic rule (multiples of 3-12, squares, cubes, primes, powers of 2-10), yes rate for non-example targets satisfying only a consistent digit rule minus targets satisfying only a consistent arithmetic rule (e.g. 8,80,48: 28/68 vs 96; 28,98: x8 vs multiples of 7); observed above null means people favour digit rules over equally-consistent arithmetic rules more than the model's size-principle weighting allows.
def test_statistic(df):
    N = np.arange(1, 101)
    digit = [N % 10 == d for d in range(10)] + [np.array([str(d) in str(n) for n in N]) for d in range(10)]
    arith = [N % m == 0 for m in range(3, 13)]
    arith.append(np.isin(N, [n * n for n in range(1, 11)]))
    arith.append(np.isin(N, [n ** 3 for n in range(1, 5)]))
    arith.append(np.array([n > 1 and all(n % a for a in range(2, int(n ** 0.5) + 1)) for n in N]))
    for m in range(2, 11):
        arith.append(np.isin(N, [m ** k for k in range(1, 8) if m ** k <= 100]))
    Dg, Ar = np.array(digit), np.array(arith)
    s_arr = df["number_set"].astype(str).to_numpy()
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    dig_only = np.zeros(len(df), bool); ar_only = np.zeros(len(df), bool)
    for s in np.unique(s_arr):
        e = np.array([int(x) for x in s.split(",")])
        dc = Dg[:, e - 1].all(axis=1); ac = Ar[:, e - 1].all(axis=1)
        if not dc.any() or not ac.any():
            continue
        dm = Dg[dc].any(axis=0); am = Ar[ac].any(axis=0)
        idx = (s_arr == s) & ~np.isin(t, e)
        dig_only |= idx & dm[t - 1] & ~am[t - 1]
        ar_only |= idx & am[t - 1] & ~dm[t - 1]
    if dig_only.sum() == 0 or ar_only.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[dig_only].mean() - r[ar_only].mean())

results.name: within_set_target_spread
results.description: Mean, over sets tested with >=8 distinct targets, of the standard deviation of per-target yes rates within the set; observed below null means people discriminate among a set's targets less sharply than the model (flatter generalization), above null means more sharply (more all-or-none).
